verdict.rationale: Docs show Codex plugins are built on MCP under the hood ("add MCP server wiring for the plugin", codex-plugins-docs-15) and that plugins/marketplace sources can be added via `codex plugin marketplace add` instead of hand-editing `config.toml` (codex-plugins-docs-11), implying a config path where MCP servers can be registered; the `/plugins` browser (codex-plugins-docs-6) lets users install and enable third-party plugins (Gmail, Drive, Slack, Notion, Figma, etc.) that presumably expose tools via MCP. However, there is no explicit first-party or independent documentation showing a user directly pointing Codex at an arbitrary/custom MCP server endpoint (vs. installing a pre-packaged plugin), and no hands-on confirmation of raw MCP-server interoperability. missing for 10: explicit doc/example of adding a custom/arbitrary MCP server (not just curated plugins), independent hands-on verification that arbitrary MCP tools work end-to-end.
